query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The range of phases observed upon cooling and subsequent thermal exposure of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 originates from a thermal activation of local chemical ordering instabilities within the initial high‐temperature BCC state. These instabilities promote heterogeneous nucleation of ordered nano-domains (e.g., B2 or other intermetallic-like regions) that subsequently grow into secondary phases under thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC state
generation.intervention: Control the cooling rate from high temperature followed by systematic thermal exposures at incremental temperatures and hold times
generation.conditions: This mechanism should apply when the alloy is cooled at rates which allow only limited atomic diffusion (producing a metastable BCC) and then subjected to thermal exposures at temperatures high enough to activate diffusion and atomic rearrangement but low enough so that the original BCC structure is not fully re-equilibrated. Under extreme rapid quenching (or at temperatures where diffusion remains frozen) no ordered phase nucleation is expected.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering (LCO) and associated atomic-scale compositional fluctuations, particularly at grain boundaries and within sub-grain regions
generation.mechanism: Upon cooling from the high-temperature BCC state, localized fluctuations in composition lead to the incipient formation of ordered clusters. Subsequent thermal exposure activates diffusion, thereby accelerating the growth and coarsening of these ordered regions into distinct secondary phases. The process is mediated by the balance between thermodynamic driving forces for ordering and the kinetic barriers to diffusion in this multi-principal element alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that are cooled slowly (or held isothermally during cooling) will exhibit a higher volume fraction of secondary, ordered phases (with clear lattice symmetry differences from the BCC parent phase) compared to rapidly cooled samples that remain predominantly metastable BCC. Additionally, thermal exposures at intermediate temperatures should induce a detectable evolution of nanoscale ordering as revealed by TEM and XRD, while exposures outside the activation window (too low or too high) will not produce the same phase diversity.
generation.baseline: Rapidly cooled Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples with minimal thermal exposure will retain a largely homogeneous, metastable BCC phase without significant formation of ordered secondary phases.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where diffusion is moderately activated (i.e., specific thermal exposure temperatures/times) and may not be valid if cooling is so rapid that no LCO can develop, or if the thermal exposure is above temperatures where complete homogenization or melting of incipient ordered clusters occurs.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature, identity, and spatial distribution of the ordered phases (e.g., whether they are B2, intermetallic, or other ordered variants) and the quantitative kinetics of LCO development remain uncertain and require further detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples using controlled cooling protocols (rapid quench and slow cooling) followed by isothermal annealing at several intermediate temperatures. Characterize the microstructure using X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess the presence and evolution of ordered nano-domains. Compare the volume fractions and size distributions of any secondary phases between cooling conditions.
measurements: Quantitative XRD phase analysis to determine phase fractions
TEM imaging (with selected area diffraction) to identify local ordering
EDS mapping to detect compositional fluctuations associated with the ordered regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no significant difference in the formation or evolution of ordered secondary phases between the rapidly quenched and slowly cooled samples upon subsequent thermal exposure, or if no evidence of local chemical ordering is detected by microscopic techniques, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Among the various systems of alloying elements studied, the Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 alloy seems to be attractive due to its reduced density of 9.94 g/cm 3 [ [2] , [3] ], few publications [ [4] , [5] , [6] ] deal with thr thermodynamic properties of certain compositions of the Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti.
